title: Blood Alcohol Calculator: Estimate Your BAC (Widmark Formula)
excerpt: Estimate your blood alcohol content with the Widmark formula, BAC charts by weight and number of drinks, worked examples, and why no calculator can tell you it's safe to drive.
metaDescription: Estimate your blood alcohol level with the Widmark formula, BAC charts by weight and drinks, and how long it takes to sober up. Never use it to drive.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The quick answer:** you can estimate your blood alcohol concentration (BAC) with the Widmark formula, which scientists have used since the 1930s. Take the grams of alcohol you drank, divide by your body weight in grams times a body-water factor (about 0.68 for men and 0.55 for women), multiply by 100, then subtract about 0.015 for every hour since you started drinking. The tables and worked examples below do the math for you. The result is a rough estimate, often off by a wide margin for any one person, and it can never tell you whether you are safe or legal to drive.

> **Never use a BAC calculator to decide whether you can drive.** Every estimate in this guide is an average. Your real BAC can be noticeably higher than the number a formula gives you, and you can be impaired, and arrested, below the legal limit. If you have been drinking, don't drive. Get a ride, call a taxi or rideshare, or wait until the next day. **Call 911 right away** if someone who has been drinking can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, is vomiting while drowsy or passed out, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and it is an emergency. Don't leave them to "sleep it off."

## How to Calculate Your Blood Alcohol Content (the Widmark Formula)

In 1932 the Swedish scientist Erik Widmark published a simple way to estimate how much alcohol ends up in your blood. Nearly every online BAC calculator, and the back-calculation methods some forensic labs use, still start from his formula. Here it is in plain terms:

**BAC (%) = [grams of alcohol ÷ (body weight in grams × r)] × 100 − (0.015 × hours since your first drink)**

Each piece means something simple:

- **Grams of alcohol** is the pure alcohol you drank. In the US, one standard drink holds about 14 grams.
- **Body weight in grams** is your weight in kilograms times 1,000 (or your weight in pounds times 453.6).
- **r** is the "Widmark factor." It reflects how much of your body is water, because alcohol spreads through body water, not fat. The commonly used averages are about **0.68 for men** and **0.55 for women**.
- **0.015 per hour** is the average rate an adult's body clears alcohol from the blood. Real people fall roughly between 0.010 and 0.020 or more per hour.

The result is a percentage. A BAC of 0.08% means 0.08 grams of alcohol per 100 milliliters of blood, which is the legal driving limit in most of the US.

### The shortcut: how much one drink raises your BAC

If you don't want to do the full math, there is an easy shortcut. One US standard drink raises BAC by roughly:

**1.4 ÷ (your weight in kg × r)**

For a 160-pound (72.6 kg) man, that is 1.4 ÷ (72.6 × 0.68), or about **0.028** per drink. For a 140-pound (63.5 kg) woman, it is 1.4 ÷ (63.5 × 0.55), or about **0.040** per drink. Multiply by the number of drinks, subtract 0.015 for each hour since you started, and you have your estimate.

## Blood Alcohol Charts by Weight and Number of Drinks

These charts show the **peak estimate before any time passes**, calculated with the Widmark formula and US standard drinks. To use them, find your weight and drink count, then subtract **0.015 for every hour** since your first drink. If the result is zero or below, the formula estimates that the alcohol has cleared.

### Estimated BAC for men (r = 0.68)

| Weight | 1 drink | 2 drinks | 3 drinks | 4 drinks | 5 drinks | 6 drinks |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 120 lb | 0.038 | 0.076 | 0.113 | 0.151 | 0.189 | 0.227 |
| 140 lb | 0.032 | 0.065 | 0.097 | 0.130 | 0.162 | 0.195 |
| 160 lb | 0.028 | 0.057 | 0.085 | 0.113 | 0.142 | 0.170 |
| 180 lb | 0.025 | 0.050 | 0.076 | 0.101 | 0.126 | 0.151 |
| 200 lb | 0.023 | 0.045 | 0.068 | 0.091 | 0.113 | 0.136 |
| 240 lb | 0.019 | 0.038 | 0.057 | 0.076 | 0.095 | 0.113 |

### Estimated BAC for women (r = 0.55)

| Weight | 1 drink | 2 drinks | 3 drinks | 4 drinks | 5 drinks | 6 drinks |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 120 lb | 0.047 | 0.094 | 0.140 | 0.187 | 0.234 | 0.281 |
| 140 lb | 0.040 | 0.080 | 0.120 | 0.160 | 0.200 | 0.241 |
| 160 lb | 0.035 | 0.070 | 0.105 | 0.140 | 0.175 | 0.210 |
| 180 lb | 0.031 | 0.062 | 0.094 | 0.125 | 0.156 | 0.187 |
| 200 lb | 0.028 | 0.056 | 0.084 | 0.112 | 0.140 | 0.168 |
| 240 lb | 0.023 | 0.047 | 0.070 | 0.094 | 0.117 | 0.140 |

Two things jump out. First, the same number of drinks produces a much higher BAC in a smaller person. Second, at the same weight, women reach a higher BAC than men. Both are about how much water the alcohol has to spread through, which we cover below.

## Worked Examples: Running the Numbers Step by Step

Seeing the formula used on real situations makes it much easier to apply to your own night.

**Example 1: A 160-pound man, four beers over three hours.**
Four 12-ounce beers at 5% alcohol are four standard drinks, or 56 grams of alcohol. His body weight is 72,600 grams. 56 ÷ (72,600 × 0.68) × 100 gives a peak of about 0.113. Three hours have passed, so subtract 0.045. **Estimated BAC: about 0.068.** That is under 0.08, but well above the level where judgment and reaction time are measurably affected, and his real number could easily be higher.

**Example 2: A 140-pound woman, the same four drinks over three hours.**
56 ÷ (63,500 × 0.55) × 100 gives a peak of about 0.160. Subtract 0.045 for three hours. **Estimated BAC: about 0.115.** Same drinks, same time, and she is well over the legal limit. This is why "I can handle four beers" means very little when two people compare notes.

**Example 3: A 130-pound woman, two big restaurant glasses of wine.**
Restaurant pours are often 6 ounces or more, and many wines are 13% to 14% alcohol. Two 6-ounce glasses at 13% contain about 36 grams of alcohol, which is about 2.6 standard drinks, not two. 36 ÷ (59,000 × 0.55) × 100 gives a peak around 0.112. Even after an hour (subtract 0.015), the estimate is near **0.097**. "Two glasses of wine" can be a lot more than it sounds.

**Example 4: When will I be back to zero?**
Take your peak estimate and divide by 0.015. That is roughly how many hours it takes to clear. A peak of 0.12 works out to about eight hours. If you stopped drinking at 1 a.m. with a BAC around 0.12, the average person would still have alcohol in their blood at 8 a.m. This is how people end up over the limit on the morning drive to work.

## How Many Standard Drinks Did You Actually Have?

The weakest link in any BAC calculation is the drink count. Calculators assume "one drink" means one US standard drink, which is about **14 grams of pure alcohol**. According to the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), that equals:

- **12 ounces of regular beer** at about 5% alcohol
- **5 ounces of table wine** at about 12% alcohol
- **1.5 ounces of distilled spirits** (one shot) at about 40% alcohol, or 80 proof

Real drinks often don't match those sizes. You can count any drink yourself:

**Standard drinks = ounces × ABV (as a decimal) × 0.79 × 29.57 ÷ 14**

Or use the simpler version: **(ounces × ABV percentage ÷ 100) ÷ 0.6**. That works because one US standard drink holds about 0.6 fluid ounces of pure alcohol. For example, a 12-ounce beer at 5% gives 12 × 5 ÷ 100 = 0.6 ounces of alcohol, and 0.6 ÷ 0.6 = 1 drink. A 16-ounce pint at 7% gives 1.12 ounces of alcohol, or almost 1.9 drinks.

| What you ordered | Approximate standard drinks |
|---|---|
| 16 oz pint of 7% IPA | about 1.9 |
| 12 oz can of 8% hard seltzer or craft beer | about 1.6 |
| 9 oz "large" glass of 13.5% wine | about 2.0 |
| Margarita with 3 oz of tequila | about 2.0 |
| Long Island iced tea (several spirits) | often 2 to 3 or more |
| 750 ml bottle of 13% wine | about 5.5 |

If a calculator says you are at 0.05 after "three drinks" but those were three pints of strong IPA, you are really closer to six drinks' worth of alcohol, and your BAC estimate should roughly double.

## Why Your Real BAC Can Differ From Any Calculator

The Widmark formula is a good average. It is not a measurement. Studies comparing formula estimates with measured blood levels have found that individual results can swing by a wide margin in either direction, which is why no responsible calculator should be used for legal or safety decisions. Here is what pushes your real number up or down.

### Food in your stomach

Eating before or while drinking is the biggest single thing you control. Food keeps alcohol in the stomach longer, so it reaches the small intestine (where most of it is absorbed) more slowly. Controlled studies have consistently found that drinking after a meal gives a lower and later peak than drinking on an empty stomach, and part of the alcohol may be broken down before it ever reaches your blood. The Widmark formula assumes all the alcohol is absorbed, so it tends to fit empty-stomach drinking better than a night out with dinner. For more on why empty-stomach drinking hits harder, see our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach).

### Body composition, not just weight

Alcohol dissolves in water, and muscle holds far more water than fat. Two people who weigh the same can have quite different BACs if one carries much more body fat. That's also the main reason women tend to reach higher BACs: on average, they have a lower percentage of body water. Some research also suggests women break down slightly less alcohol in the stomach before it is absorbed, though that finding is less settled. More detailed formulas, such as the Watson method that estimates total body water from height, weight, age and sex, can fit individual people a little better than a single r value.

### How fast you drink

The tables above assume you drank everything at once. Spreading the same drinks over more hours lets your liver clear some alcohol as you go. Pounding shots or chugging drinks pushes the peak higher and faster, because absorption outruns elimination.

### Your elimination rate

The 0.015 per hour figure is an average. Some people clear alcohol more slowly, around 0.010 per hour, and people who drink heavily on a regular basis often clear it faster because their liver enzymes have adapted. A faster rate doesn't mean less harm; it reflects a body that has adjusted to a lot of alcohol. If you want the details on what actually changes that rate (and what doesn't), our article on [how to speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism) separates the science from the myths.

### Medications and health conditions

Some medications can change how alcohol is absorbed or how strongly it affects you, and many add their own drowsiness on top of alcohol's. Liver disease slows alcohol clearance. Carbonated mixers may speed absorption a little. If you take any regular medication, ask a pharmacist how it combines with alcohol rather than relying on a calculator.

### Genetics

Variations in alcohol-processing enzymes, common in people of East Asian descent, change how quickly alcohol and its toxic breakdown product, acetaldehyde, are handled. That affects how you feel more than the BAC number itself, but it is another reason identical BACs can feel very different from person to person. Our guide to [alcohol metabolism and genetic testing](/never-hungover/alcohol-metabolism-genetic-testing-complete-personalized-health-guide-2025) explains these variants.

## Your BAC Keeps Rising After Your Last Drink

This catches a lot of people out. Alcohol takes time to move from your stomach and intestine into your blood. On an empty stomach, BAC usually peaks somewhere around 30 to 90 minutes after your last drink, and it can take longer after a big meal. That means:

- The BAC you have when you leave the bar may be **lower than the BAC you'll have 30 to 60 minutes later**, when you're behind the wheel.
- "Last call" drinks, especially fast ones, keep pushing your level up after you stop.
- Someone who seems "fine" when they stop drinking can become much more impaired, or dangerously ill, over the next hour. That's why you should never leave a very drunk person alone to sleep.

## What Different BAC Levels Feel Like

These are typical effects for an average adult without a high tolerance, based on descriptions used by the NIAAA and US traffic safety agencies. Tolerance can hide the outward signs, but it does not protect your reaction time or judgment as much as it feels like it does.

| BAC | Typical effects |
|---|---|
| 0.02 to 0.03 | Mild relaxation and warmth. Some loss of judgment and a slight drop in the ability to track moving objects and do two things at once. |
| 0.05 to 0.06 | Lowered inhibitions, louder and more talkative. Slower reactions and reduced coordination. Driving risk is clearly higher. |
| 0.08 | The legal driving limit in most of the US. Poorer muscle coordination, balance, speech, vision and hearing. Judgment, self-control and memory are affected. |
| 0.10 to 0.12 | Clear slowing of reaction time, slurred speech, poor coordination. |
| 0.15 to 0.20 | Major loss of balance and control, vomiting is possible. Blackouts (gaps in memory) become more likely. |
| 0.25 to 0.30 | Severe confusion, stupor, risk of choking on vomit. Alcohol poisoning territory. |
| 0.30 and above | Possible loss of consciousness, slowed breathing and heart rate. Can be fatal. |

Remember that these levels describe the average person. Smaller people, people who haven't eaten, and people who don't drink often can feel these effects at lower numbers.

## What Is the Legal BAC Limit?

In the United States, it is illegal to drive with a BAC of **0.08% or higher** in every state except **Utah**, where the limit has been **0.05%** since the end of 2018. A few other rules matter:

- **Commercial drivers** (such as truck and bus drivers) are held to **0.04%** while operating commercial vehicles.
- **Drivers under 21** face "zero tolerance" laws in every state, usually set at 0.00% to 0.02%.
- **You can be charged below the limit.** If police judge that you are impaired, a DUI charge doesn't require you to be at 0.08.
- **Many other countries are stricter.** Much of Europe and Australia use 0.05%, and some countries set limits near zero.

The legal limit is not a "safe" line. Crash risk starts rising at levels well below 0.08, which is part of why the National Transportation Safety Board has recommended lowering the US limit to 0.05.

## Are Online BAC Calculators Accurate?

They are accurate in the sense that they do the Widmark math correctly. They are not accurate in the sense of telling you your actual BAC. The formula ignores food, absorption speed, body composition and your personal elimination rate, and it depends on you remembering exactly what and how much you drank, which is hardest to do when you've been drinking.

A good rule is to treat any calculator result as **a floor for your worry, not a ceiling**. If the estimate is near the limit, you could be over it. If it says you'll be "sober by 6 a.m.," plan on later.

### What about breathalyzers?

Personal breathalyzers measure alcohol in your breath and convert it to an estimated BAC. Police-grade devices are calibrated and tested regularly; cheap consumer models vary a lot in accuracy. Readings can be thrown off by "mouth alcohol" if you drank, used mouthwash, burped or vomited in the last 15 minutes or so. A consumer breathalyzer can be a useful reality check that you're higher than you think, but a low reading isn't proof you're fine to drive. Our guide to [at-home alcohol testing](/never-hungover/at-home-alcohol-testing-monitoring-safety-guide-2025) covers the device types in more detail.

## Will I Still Be Drunk in the Morning?

Quite possibly. Using the average rate of 0.015 per hour, it takes about five to six hours to clear a BAC of 0.08, and about ten hours to clear 0.15. If you were drinking heavily until late, there is a real chance you're still over the limit when your alarm goes off, even after a full night's sleep.

Sleep doesn't speed this up. Neither do coffee, cold showers, exercise or a greasy breakfast. Coffee can make you feel more alert, but a wide-awake drunk person is still impaired. Only time brings BAC down.

There is also a difference between your BAC reaching zero and you feeling normal. A hangover usually peaks around the time your BAC returns to zero, and it can keep you foggy and slow for many hours after that. Our guide on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) explains the timeline.

## How to Keep Your BAC Lower on a Night Out

You can't change the formula, but you can change the inputs:

- **Eat a real meal before you start**, ideally with protein, fat and fiber, and keep snacking.
- **Count in standard drinks**, not glasses. Check the ABV of craft beers and the size of wine pours.
- **Pace yourself.** Aim for no more than about one standard drink per hour, and remember that's roughly what an average body clears.
- **Alternate with water** or a non-alcoholic drink. It slows your pace and helps with hydration.
- **Skip shots and drinking games**, which push your peak up fastest.
- **Decide your ride home before the first drink**, so you're not making that choice with a raised BAC.

The NIAAA defines binge drinking as a pattern that brings BAC to 0.08 or higher, which for a typical adult means about four drinks for women or five for men in about two hours. Staying well under those numbers keeps your BAC lower, cuts your risk of harm, and also makes the next morning much easier.

## Signs of Alcohol Poisoning: When a BAC Number Doesn't Matter

If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, don't try to calculate their BAC. Act. Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if a person who has been drinking:

- Can't be woken up, or is very hard to wake
- Is confused or stuporous
- Is vomiting, especially while drowsy or passed out
- Has a seizure
- Is breathing slowly (fewer than about eight breaths a minute) or irregularly, with long pauses
- Has pale, bluish, cold or clammy skin
- Has a very low body temperature

While you wait for help, stay with them. If they're lying down, roll them onto their side so they won't choke if they vomit. Don't give them coffee or a cold shower, and don't let them "sleep it off." BAC can keep rising after they pass out.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

It's worth being clear about this, because supplements are sometimes marketed as if they can "lower your BAC." **There is no good evidence that DHM (dihydromyricetin) or any other supplement lowers your blood alcohol level enough to matter for driving or safety.** Nothing you take changes the advice above: if you've been drinking, don't drive.

What DHM is studied for is different. It is a plant compound that researchers have looked at for its effects on how the body processes alcohol and its by-products, and on how people feel the next day. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it is promising rather than settled. Some people who drink socially take it on nights out as part of a broader plan of eating, pacing and hydrating. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [guide to preventing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## The Bottom Line

- The Widmark formula estimates BAC from drinks, body weight, sex and time: grams of alcohol ÷ (weight in grams × 0.68 for men or 0.55 for women) × 100, minus 0.015 per hour.
- One standard drink raises BAC by roughly 0.02 to 0.05 depending on your size and sex, and the average body clears about 0.015 per hour.
- Real BAC can be noticeably higher or lower than any estimate because of food, drinking speed, body composition, medications and personal metabolism.
- BAC keeps rising for up to an hour or more after your last drink, and only time brings it down.
- Never use a calculator to decide whether to drive. If you've been drinking, find another way home, and call 911 for any signs of alcohol poisoning.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How do you calculate blood alcohol content?**

Use the Widmark formula: divide the grams of alcohol you drank by your body weight in grams times a body-water factor (about 0.68 for men and 0.55 for women), multiply by 100, then subtract about 0.015 for each hour since your first drink. One US standard drink holds about 14 grams of alcohol. The result is only an estimate and can be noticeably off for any one person.

**How much does one drink raise your BAC?**

Roughly 0.02 to 0.05, depending on your weight and sex. A 160-pound man goes up about 0.028 per standard drink, and a 140-pound woman about 0.040. Smaller people and people drinking on an empty stomach tend to land at the higher end.

**How long does it take for BAC to go down?**

The average adult clears about 0.015 BAC per hour, though people range from roughly 0.010 to 0.020 or more. At the average rate, a BAC of 0.08 takes about five to six hours to reach zero, and 0.15 takes about ten. Sleep, coffee, water, cold showers and exercise don't speed it up. Only time does.

**How many drinks does it take to reach 0.08?**

For an average 160-pound man, about three standard drinks in quick succession puts the estimate near 0.085. For an average 140-pound woman, about two drinks gets close to 0.08. Food, pace and body composition shift these numbers a lot, which is why you should never count drinks to decide whether you can drive.

**Are online BAC calculators accurate?**

They do the math correctly, but they can't measure your actual BAC. They ignore food, how fast you drank, your body composition and your personal elimination rate, and they rely on you counting drinks accurately. Treat any result as a rough guide, assume your real BAC could be higher, and never use one to decide whether to drive.

**Why do women reach a higher BAC than men?**

On average, women have a lower percentage of body water, and alcohol spreads through body water. The same amount of alcohol ends up more concentrated in the blood. That's why BAC formulas use a lower factor for women (about 0.55 versus 0.68 for men), and why the same number of drinks gives a woman a higher estimate at the same weight.

**Can I still be over the limit the next morning?**

Yes. If you drank heavily until late, your BAC may still be above zero, or even above the legal limit, when you wake up. At an average clearance of 0.015 per hour, a BAC of 0.12 at 1 a.m. would take until about 9 a.m. to clear. If you had a heavy night, don't drive early the next morning.

**Does DHM lower your blood alcohol level?**

There is no good evidence that DHM or any supplement lowers your BAC enough to matter for driving or safety. DHM is studied for how it affects alcohol processing and how people feel the next day, mostly in animal and lab research. It does not change the rule: if you've been drinking, don't drive.
